title: Freya and the Visitor
premise: Bram Ravensworth, a hospice nurse who records his dying patients' final nights, notices they all count backwards from the same number—and that a second voice on the tapes answers their questions. When he traces the voice to Marigold House, the estate funding his hospice, he learns the family has kept an invited guest fed for two centuries through contracts signed by the dying. As the last resident, elderly Edith Vane, nears her signature, Bram must choose between exposing the truth and protecting the woman he's come to love as a daughter—knowing the Visitor only honors what is freely given. At sunrise after the longest night of his life, Bram convinces Edith to sign her house to no one, starving the invitation, and the Visitor turns its attention to him instead; he survives only because he offers it the one thing it cannot refuse: to be remembered honestly, documented in his own hand.
about_author: Beatrix Lockridge is the pen name of a former palliative care chaplain who spent eleven years listening to last words and now writes horror about what people say when no one is supposed to be listening. She lives in coastal Maine, where she keeps a tape recorder running at night purely out of professional habit.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: POV Bram. On night shift at Larkspur Hospice, Bram documents patient Harold counting backwards from 144 in his sleep, precise and unafraid. Bram's ritual of recording everything is framed as devotion, not science. Emotional beat: quiet unease beneath professional calm—the reader learns documentation is how Bram keeps grief at arm's length.

chapters.title: Second Voice
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Reviewing the overnight tape, Bram hears a low, courteous voice answer Harold's questions between counts. The voice knows things Harold never told anyone. Bram tells himself it's bleed-through from another room. Emotional beat: denial curdling into obsession; he replays the tape until dawn.

chapters.title: What the Dying Ask
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Over three nights, three different patients ask the second voice the same question: 'Did I get to choose?' Each receives a gentle yes. Bram cross-references old recordings and finds the pattern goes back years. Emotional beat: dread of complicity—he has been present at these conversations all along, silent.

chapters.title: Edith Vane Signs Nothing
chapters.summary: POV Edith. The hospice's last resident, sharp-tongued Edith, refuses the paperwork a solicitor keeps sending from Marigold House, the estate that funds the facility. She teases Bram but watches him too closely. Emotional beat: warmth and suspicion braided together; Edith knows more than she says.

chapters.title: Marigold House
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Following an address on the solicitor's letterhead, Bram finds Marigold House immaculate and empty, its ledgers open on a table showing payments to the hospice dating to 1798—all triggered by deaths. A caretaker tells him the family 'keeps an arrangement.' Emotional beat: awe tipping into violation; charity revealed as feeding.

chapters.title: The Invitation Clause
chapters.summary: POV Bram. In the county archive, Bram reads the original covenant: the entity was invited in willingly by the first Lady Vane, and can only take what is signed over freely at the end of life. Every contract since renews the welcome. Emotional beat: horrified clarity—the hospice itself is part of the trap.

chapters.title: Harold's Last Question
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Harold dies at 3:11 a.m., mid-count, and the second voice says, 'Thank you for your hospitality' directly toward the recorder—as if it knows Bram listens. Bram plays the tape for his supervisor, who hears nothing but static. Emotional beat: isolation; the truth makes him invisible again, which he swore he'd stopped being.

chapters.title: Loyalty of Small Hours
chapters.summary: POV Edith. Edith recalls her own mother's deathbed signing and the cold gratitude in the room afterward. She recognizes in Bram the same look she wore at nineteen: someone about to learn the family business. Emotional beat: tenderness hardening into resolve—she decides Bram must not inherit this alone.

chapters.title: The Solicitor's Visit
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Mr. Quill, the solicitor, visits the hospice with Edith's final papers and a smile that doesn't reach his eyes. He warns Bram off 'sentimental interference,' noting how well the hospice pays its staff. Emotional beat: temptation made explicit—Bram's whole fragile world is funded by the thing he fears.

chapters.title: Tape 144
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Bram isolates the voice digitally and matches it to a 1974 recording of Edith's mother—same voice, same cadence, decades apart. It isn't imitating the dead; the dead were rehearsing it. Emotional beat: vertigo of identity—the Visitor wears the voices of everyone it has eaten kindly.

chapters.title: Love Against the Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Edith. Edith asks Bram to burn her copy of the contract; he refuses, insisting truth must survive even if she doesn't. They fight, then confess what they actually fear: being forgotten without having been known. Emotional beat: love declared sideways, through argument, in a hospice kitchen at 4 a.m.

chapters.title: Quill Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Quill offers Bram a position at Marigold House—archivist of the dying, keeper of the tapes—with his debts erased. The Visitor, Quill implies, admires documentarians. Emotional beat: the horror of being seen exactly as you are, and offered a crown for it.

chapters.title: The Long Night Begins
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Edith's decline accelerates; doctors give her days. Quill schedules the signing for dawn. Bram realizes the timing: the Visitor wants the papers executed before sunrise, when its claim must renew. Emotional beat: countdown pressure; every hour of the shift becomes a siege.

chapters.title: Voices in the Corridors
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Overnight, the hospice fills with sounds of former residents counting, walking, thanking Bram by name. The staff hear nothing. The Visitor demonstrates it can unmake his credibility with one word to the wrong ear. Emotional beat: gaslit terror—his evidence is real and useless.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Edith. Edith tells Bram she was meant to sign forty years ago and fled, and that her long life since has been borrowed time the Visitor patiently allowed. She asks him not to save her, but to witness her. Emotional beat: grace—dignity reclaimed through honest telling rather than escape.

chapters.title: The Signature Room
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Quill arrives early with witnesses; the room grows cold and crowded with presences only Bram perceives. Edith's pen hovers. Bram, forbidden to interfere, begins reading the covenant aloud, exposing its terms to everyone present. Emotional beat: defiance—truth deployed as a weapon in real time.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: POV Bram. The Visitor manifests wearing the accumulated voices of two centuries of the dying and addresses Bram directly: it knows his recordings, his loneliness, his wish to matter. It offers to let Edith die in peace if Bram signs as successor archivist. Emotional beat: the climax of temptation—love against duty at knife-point.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: POV Edith. As the sky lightens, Edith takes the pen—but signs a new document Bram drafted: her house willed to the hospice outright, no covenant, no renewal. The invitation lapses. The room's cold breaks like ice. Emotional beat: triumph purchased with terrible cost, as the Visitor's attention swings fully onto Bram.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: POV Bram. With its contract void, the Visitor cannot take Edith—but it can haunt Bram, who now hears it counting in his own apartment, patient as winter. He understands the price of his victory will be paid across the rest of his life. Emotional beat: hollowed-out courage; survival reframed as sentence.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Prayer
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Bram makes his counter-offer: he will record the Visitor faithfully—its history, its hunger, its two hundred years of consented taking—in a book the world can read. Being truly known, he gambles, is the one thing it has never been given. Emotional beat: desperate empathy as strategy; the nurse's instinct turned exorcism.

chapters.title: Freya
chapters.summary: POV Bram. The Visitor gives its true name—Freya, the first Lady Vane herself, transformed by what she invited—and weeps in a voice like Harold's. Accepted witness, it recedes from Bram's nights, bound now to the pages rather than the patients. Edith dies at peace at noon. Emotional beat: grief and release entwined; the monster was the first victim.

chapters.title: The Book of Counts
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Weeks later, Bram publishes the transcripts under Beatrix Lockridge's name and resigns from the funded hospice, opening a free clinic on Edith's bequest. On quiet nights he still hears counting at the edge of hearing—and answers, once, 'You're documented now.' Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; loyalty to the dead fulfilled through truth, identity finally chosen rather than assigned.
